extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of art and architecture, and educated general readers interested in art history and criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and evaluation of Byzantine and Gothic architectural and pictorial qualities, focusing on material techniques (mosaic, marble, color), symbolic motifs, and the mental/formal elements that constitute 'Gothicness.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Golden-ground mosaic ornament (glass leaf-gilded tesserae)
rubrics_metrics.description: The general effect of these ornaments when seen in shadow against light; obtained by the use of a golden ground formed of glass mosaic inserted in the hollows of the marble. Each square of glass has the leaf gold upon its surface protected by another thin film of glass above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Visual effect: in shadow the perfectly reflective golden surface 'refuses the darkness' and shows bright light behind darker traceries; in sunshine the white marble appears as snowy tracery on a golden ground. Practical note: mosaic is the most secure of decorations if carefully watched and refastened when it loosens, but if neglected and exposed to weather it may disappear and leave no vestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of veined/colored marble contrasted with pure white sculpture and gilding
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the shafts of the pillars and the facing of the old building were of veined or variously colored marble: the capitals and sculptures were either of pure white marble relieved upon the veined ground, or grounded in richer palaces with mosaic of gold, in inferior ones with blue color; and only the leaves and edges of the sculpture gilded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Color/texture strategy: contrast pale delicate sculpture against richer veined or colored grounds to produce 'enchantments' of ornament. Complementary devices include alternate bands of deeper color (generally russet and green) in archivolts, and circular disks of green serpentine and porphyry as recurring Eastern-derived ornaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eastern decorative preferences (bands of color and circular inlays)
rubrics_metrics.description: Brighter hues were opposed by bands of deeper color, generally alternate russet and green, in the archivolts, and by circular disks of green serpentine and porphyry, which ... appear to have been an ornament peculiarly grateful to the Eastern mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognition: look for alternating colored bands and inlaid disks as markers of Eastern/Byzantine decorative influence; historically derived from practices like suspending shields upon the wall.

rubrics_metrics.name: Symbolic use of sculptural motifs (peacock, vine, dove, contending animals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many minor sculptural subjects have meanings familiar to early Christianity: the peacock is the well-known symbol of the resurrection (and when drinking from a fountain or font a type of new life in baptism); the vine is a type of Christ or of those in union with him; the dove represents the coming of the Comforter; groups of contending animals probably refer to powers of evil.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: read recurring fauna and botanical motifs as theological or liturgical symbols rather than mere ornament; such symbolism marks the seriousness of the early Venetian mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color as sacred, moral, and intellectual quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Of all God's gifts to the sight of man, color is the holiest, the most divine, the most solemn. All good color is in some degree pensive, the loveliest is melancholy, and the purest and most thoughtful minds are those which love color the most.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical test: evaluate palette purity and tonal temperament as indicators of moral or intellectual depth in art. Anti-pattern: dismissing color as merely sensual; instead consider whether color contributes a serious, pensive, or sacred quality to the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Artist's religious/moral disposition reflected in colouring
rubrics_metrics.description: The more faithful and earnest the religion of the painter, the more pure and prevalent is the system of his color. So surely as a painter is irreligious, thoughtless, or obscene in disposition, so surely is his coloring cold, gloomy, and valueless.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and comparative guidance: Fra Angelico — pure, jewel-like colors; Salvator Rosa — dissipated life and gloomy grey colouring. Use an artist's palette as an index of moral/intellectual temperament when assessing works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color elevates otherwise mean or sensual painters
rubrics_metrics.description: Where color becomes a primal intention with a painter otherwise mean or sensual, it instantly elevates him, and becomes the one sacred and saving element in his work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment note: if color is the dominant, consciously-held purpose of a work, it can redeem weaknesses elsewhere; look for color as intentional, unifying force even in painters with other faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gothicness is a matter of degree: union of elements and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Every building of the Gothic period differs in some important respect from every other; all we have to reason upon is a greater or less degree of 'Gothicness' in each building. Pointed arches do not constitute Gothic, nor vaulted roofs, nor flying buttresses, nor grotesque sculptures; but all or some of these things, and many other things with them, when they come together so as to have life.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: evaluate Gothic quality by degree rather than binary presence/absence. Avoid judging solely by isolated features; consider the living union and harmony of features to assess 'how Gothic' a building is.

rubrics_metrics.name: Twofold definition strategy: Mental Expression and Material Form
rubrics_metrics.description: Gothic architecture has external forms, and internal elements. Its elements are certain mental tendencies of the builders, legibly expressed in it; as fancifulness, love of variety, love of richness, and such others. Its external forms are pointed arches, vaulted roofs, &c. And unless both the elements and the forms are there, we have no right to call the style Gothic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analytical approach: first determine the Mental Power or Expression (the spirit/intent), then the Material Form (the physical motifs). Both must be present to justify calling a building Gothic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental elements (characters) of Gothic — enumerated
rubrics_metrics.description: The characteristic or moral elements of Gothic are the following, placed in the order of their importance: 1. Savageness. 2. Changefulness. 3. Naturalism. 4. Grotesqueness. 5. Rigidity. 6. Redundance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these six as a checklist of internal tendencies. Note Ruskin's caveat: the withdrawal of any one or two elements will not destroy Gothicness, but removal of a majority will reduce it significantly; the listed order indicates relative importance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Savageness (as a central Gothic quality)
rubrics_metrics.description: Savageness (or Rudeness) — Gothic architecture is rude and wild; this character is an essential and often noble mark of Northern architecture. Not degradation but dignity; a look of mountain-brotherhood between cathedral and Alp; magnificent sturdy power like that of men who cleave the forest and break the rock for bread.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: view roughness, forceful forms, and 'wolfish life' as positive indicators of authentic Gothic spirit, reflecting climate, labor, and religious seriousness. Anti-pattern: mistaking 'rude' for 'inferior' — Ruskin argues for reverence rather than condemnation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systems of ornament: servile, constitutional, revolutionary
rubrics_metrics.description: Architectural ornament systems may be divided into three: 1. Servile ornament, in which the execution or power of the inferior workman is entirely subjected to the intellect of the higher; 2. Constitutional ornament, in which the executive inferior power is, to a certain point, emancipated and independent, having a will of its own yet confessing its inferiority; and 3. Revolutionary ornament, in which no executive inferiority is admitted at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these categories to judge the social/organizational character of ornament production. Examples: Greek ornament is servile in a high-precision sense; Assyrian/Egyptian impose legal standards of imperfection; medieval/Christian practice moves toward emancipation of the workman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medieval/Christian ornament: emancipation and confession of imperfection
rubrics_metrics.description: In the mediæval, or especially Christian, system of ornament this slavery is done away with altogether: Christianity recognizes the individual value of every soul and confesses its imperfection, bestowing dignity upon the acknowledgment of unworthiness. The Christian summons each spirit to 'Do what you can, and confess frankly what you are unable to do.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative implication: look for confessed imperfection and independent execution in Gothic ornament as signs of spiritual and moral approach; judge works not by mechanical perfection but by honest labor and individual contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: External Gothic forms (examples) are necessary but not sufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: External forms of Gothic include pointed arches, vaulted roofs, flying buttresses, grotesque sculptures, &c.; but forms alone without the internal mental elements do not constitute the true Gothic style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical checklist: identify external motifs but always test them against the presence of the mental tendencies (savageness, changefulness, etc.). Beware pastiche: mere replication of forms without the 'life' is inauthentic Gothic.
